post_text:
Idempotency is simple, until it isn't.

We needed to guarantee payment webhooks processed exactly once.

I implemented the standard pattern: SELECT the event key, if not found, INSERT the new record. I felt confident in the simplicity and our standard `READ COMMITTED` isolation level. 😌

Then the Black Friday spike hit. A partner’s aggressive retry logic hammered the endpoint.

Alerts screamed about duplicate payment credits. 💸

I assumed the database transaction would serialize the check-and-write operation. It never occurred to me that two near-simultaneous requests could both execute the `SELECT` (finding nothing) before either managed to commit the subsequent `INSERT`.

The race condition window was defined by the application's synchronous lease time, not the database's internal lock mechanism. The application logic boundary was too wide.

The consequence: we had to manually reconcile hundreds of double-credited accounts, a massive operational cost. We immediately switched to using a unique constraint on the event key, forcing the database to reject duplicates atomically.

We moved the idempotency logic out of the application flow and into the schema.

The Moral 👇

The application logic boundary is wider than the database transaction boundary; atomic enforcement belongs to the constraint layer.
